identification.summary: Russian-speaking, financially motivated ransomware group that Group-IB (as reported by the press) describes as unusual because it mainly attacks Russian organizations, which most Russian-speaking ransomware operators avoid [S1][S2]. Group-IB's first public reporting was in September 2020 and dated campaigns to spring 2020 [S1]. Kaspersky reported renewed activity in early 2025 [S6].
identification.firstObserved: Spring 2020 (campaigns since about March 2020 per Group-IB's 2022 reporting [S4]; first reported by Group-IB in September 2020 [S1]).
identification.notes: Group-IB also tracks the group as TinyScouts [S2][S4]. Coverage of the 2022 Linux report and of Brandefense's 2025 write-up differs on geographic scope: Group-IB-derived reporting describes mainly Russian targets [S2][S4], while Brandefense says Europe and the Americas are also targeted [S7]; the Brandefense claim is not corroborated by other gathered sources. The 2025 Kaspersky ransom-note use of the 'OldGremlin' name is reported as the first time the operators used the name themselves [S6].

attribution.confidence: Vendors describe the group as financially motivated and Russian-speaking [S1][S2][S6]. No government or state sponsorship attribution was found in gathered sources. Kaspersky links its 2025 incidents to earlier OldGremlin campaigns via consistent tactics and a reused cryptographic public key (Kaspersky's own assessment, as reported) [S6].
attribution.basis: Group-IB analysis of 2020-2022 campaigns (via press coverage) [S1][S2]; Kaspersky Threat Research on 2025 activity (via press-release coverage) [S6].

objectives: Financial gain through large-scale ransomware extortion; Group-IB-derived reporting gives a maximum demand of $4.2 million in 2021 and $16.9 million in 2022 [S2][S4]. Kaspersky's 2025 report mentions the group earlier demanded nearly $17 million from one victim [S6].

targeting.notes: 2020 reporting: medical labs, banks, manufacturers and software developers [S1]. 2022: logistics, industry, insurance, retail, real estate, software development, banking [S2][S4]. 2025: manufacturing, healthcare, retail and technology [S6]. Brandefense claims Europe and the Americas as well [S7] (uncorroborated).

capabilities.summary: Targeted phishing email as initial access, with lures such as an invoice purporting to come from RBC and COVID-themed mails impersonating a Russian microfinance organization [S1]. A link downloads a ZIP containing the custom TinyNode backdoor or the TinyPosh trojan [S1]. Cobalt Strike is used for lateral movement, followed by domain admin credential theft, creation of a privileged account for persistence, deletion of server backups and encryption with TinyCryptor (aka decr1pt) several weeks after the attack began [S1]. A Go-built Linux variant of the TinyCrypt ransomware (AES-256-CBC, .crypt extension) was found in 2022 [S4]. Kaspersky's 2025 toolkit comprises a backdoor, a 'patcher' abusing a flaw in a legitimate Windows driver to disable protections, an encryptor, and a 'closethedoor' tool to isolate the host and remove traces, with Node.js used to run commands; typical dwell time before encryption is about 49 days [S6].

campaigns.name: Initial phishing campaigns (TinyNode/TinyCryptor)
campaigns.summary: Group-IB reports custom-tool operations (nine campaigns between May and August 2020 per the Sept 2020 report [S1]; Group-IB's later reporting counts activity since March 2020 [S4]) against Russian medical labs, banks, manufacturers and software developers; a successful attack in August 2020 hit a clinical diagnostics lab. Ransom demand cited at $50,000 in cryptocurrency.

campaigns.name: Retail-association impersonation campaign
campaigns.summary: Coverage of Group-IB reporting describes a single 2021 campaign in which the actor impersonated an association of online retailers; maximum demand that year was $4.2 million.

campaigns.name: Linux TinyCrypt variant and record demand
campaigns.summary: Group-IB reported a Go-built Linux version of TinyCrypt and a maximum ransom demand of $16.9 million in 2022; targets spanned logistics, industry, insurance, retail, real estate, software and banking.

campaigns.name: Return in 2025
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reported new attacks from early 2025 against manufacturing, healthcare, retail and technology firms, with a new toolkit, about 49 days of dwell time, and first use of the 'OldGremlin' name in ransom notes and file paths.

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking financially motivated ransomware group, also tracked by Group-IB as TinyScouts [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Phishing, custom backdoors (TinyNode, TinyPosh), Cobalt Strike, TinyCryptor/TinyCrypt ransomware for Windows and Linux, BYOVD-style driver abuse in 2025 [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Phishing links hosting ZIP payloads [S1]; specific infrastructure details were not obtained.
diamond.victim: Mainly Russian banks, industrial, medical, software, logistics, insurance and retail organizations [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial extortion against Russian entities, atypical for Russian-speaking ransomware actors [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows and Linux enterprise networks reachable through email; Active Directory domain credentials; backups targeted for deletion [S1][S4].

gaps: Direct fetches of Group-IB, Kaspersky, The Hacker News and BleepingComputer pages failed in this environment; content relies on search-result summaries of those reports, and primary documents were not opened.
Year of the $16.9 million demand and details of the 2021 campaign come from secondary coverage [S4].
No sponsor, individuals, or law-enforcement action identified in gathered sources.
Brandefense claim of non-Russian targeting is uncorroborated [S7].
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID or Microsoft name was identified.
Initial access broker relationships, infrastructure and IOCs not gathered.
Hackread and Security Affairs URLs could not be confirmed in search results; those sources and the TinyFluff (2022) claims resting on them were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways, domain controllers and backup systems are key terrain in organizations the group targets [S1]. STEP 2: The group primarily victimizes Russian entities, so direct relevance to US/allied networks is limited and mainly as a model of criminal intrusion tradecraft [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is phishing, custom backdoor, Cobalt Strike, domain-admin theft, backup deletion, then long-dwell encryption (about 49 days in 2025) on Windows and Linux [S1][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-volume, high-demand ransomware against Russian industry. MDCOA is expansion to non-Russian organizations, as one unverified vendor claim suggests [S7]. Candidate indicators: phishing mail with ZIP links impersonating trade bodies, Cobalt Strike beacons, new privileged accounts, loading of vulnerable Windows drivers, mass backup deletion [S1][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Long dwell time (about 49 days) gives a detection window; feed backup-deletion and new-admin-account alerts into situational awareness [S1][S6]. (2) Mission assurance: protect offline backups and Linux servers, since a Linux encryptor exists [S4]. (3) Authorities and coordination: treat as criminal activity; coordinate through normal law-enforcement and DC3/industry-sharing channels if any DoD-adjacent victim emerges. Relevance is low unless targeting shifts [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: OldGremlin is a Russian-speaking ransomware group that has been active for several years. They primarily target organizations in Russia, including banks, logistics, industrial, insurance, retail, and IT companies. OldGremlin is known for using phishing emails as an initial infection vector and has developed custom malware for both Windows and Linux systems. They have conducted multiple malicious email campaigns and demand large ransoms from their victims, with some reaching millions of dollars.
